{"files":[{"canAddChildren":false,"contentSnippet":"# Product Data Science: Charter and Boundaries

## Summary

Create Product Data Science, a new team within Product/Engineering, staffed by two new hires plus my move from the Data team. The team owns the gold layer and the semantic layer, embeds with squads to shape data at design time, and staffs a narrowly scoped Data Design Review on new event streams and persisted entities.

Cost: two new hires, plus one net reduction to Data team capacity. No other transfers. The Data team's structure and scope are unchanged.

What changes for Engineering: one new review gate, scoped to new event streams and new persisted entities only, with a three-business-day SLA and silence-equals-approval for additive changes.

What Engineering gets: analytics tied directly to the products and features that produce them, rather than assembled after the fact from whatever is available. Post-hoc analysis is frequently wrong, insufficient, or carries caveats nobody surfaces. Those caveats are the expensive part, because the answer looks like every other answer. This is particularly dangerous for agentic analysis. Squads that can quantify what they ship, without an analyst in the loop.

### Alternatives considered

|  |  |
| :-: | :-: |
| Alternative | Why not |
| Run the design review gate with no new team | Data Engineers are already tagged on upstream schema changes. They have neither the business context nor knowledge of how the data will be analyzed to give critical feedback on grain, keys, or taxonomy. The gate without embedded reviewers is the review we already have. |
| Fund the Data team instead | The request-driven model is correct for Data Analytics' mission and does not produce squad context. An IC on loan to a squad is prioritized against the analytics queue and recalled when demand spikes, which is exactly when squads are shipping. |
| Re-embed existing Data team ICs | Same recall problem, plus a different mandate: Data Analytics is chartered to answer questions, and this role is chartered to make squads able to answer their own. One team holding both means the urgent job wins every time. |
| Matrix / dotted line into squads | Addresses presence but not incentives or the review norm. A reviewer accountable elsewhere signs off to whatever depth the deadline allows. |
| Do nothing until we're larger | The cost of getting grain and identifiers right is near zero at design time and enormous afterward. The datasets are arriving either way; they land shaped or unshaped. Reshaping later means migrations and backfills that are rarely possible. |

## The Need

Over the last 18 months, Runpod has built a world-class medallion architecture, tools for quickly adding new data sets to it, and a number of high-quality gold data products that can be effectively used throughout the organization. This is not a proposal to fix any of that. The current state is good because a small number of people have applied consistent standards and robust tooling without an organizational mandate to do so. That arrangement has held at Runpod's current size. It will not hold through the growth ahead — every constraint below gets materially worse as squads, datasets, stakeholders, and agents multiply.

1.  Coverage is throughput-bound, and uncovered domains are decision risk. Domains with modeled, curated coverage (i.e., gold data sets and agent skills) get fast and trustworthy answers. Domains without this structure wait for capacity, or, more often, get answered anyway from raw data that has not been validated and is not optimized for analytical use. That second path is the expensive one: it produces decisions made on poor-quality information using undefined methodologies, and it does so invisibly, because the answer looks like every other answer. As new product areas launch faster than coverage can follow, the share of the business sitting in that category grows.
2.  The standards are conventions, not policy. They are real and consistently applied, but—aside from Data Engineering and the Bronze/Silver layers—they are not written down as organizational commitments with owners and review. Growth is what converts this from a tolerable risk into a certainty.
3.  The forward constraint is the binding one. Agent-accessible data, fleet expansion analytics, and squad self-service all require modeled coverage in domains that don't have it, plus semantic metadata that nothing currently produces. The next phases of workload allocation are a concrete case: they will be data-driven, and they depend on exactly the rigor and cross-team collaboration the sections below formalize. These are capabilities Runpod doesn't have yet — not risks it's carrying — and the bar rises with growth.
4.  The volume arrives whether or not the team exists. Runpod is entering a phase of rapid growth, with new product squads and new datasets emerging faster than at any prior point. ## What this document is for

Over the last 18 months, Runpod has built a world-class medallion architecture, tools for quickly adding new data sets to it, and a number of high-quality gold data products that can be effectively used throughout the organization.

That is the argument, not a caveat to it. The current state is good because a small number of people applied consistent standards and robust tooling without an organizational mandate to do so. That arrangement has held at Runpod's current size. It will not hold through the growth ahead — every constraint below gets materially worse as squads, datasets, and stakeholders multiply.

1.  Coverage is throughput-bound, and uncovered domains are decision risk. Domains with modeled, curated coverage (i.e., gold data sets and agent skills) get fast and trustworthy answers. Domains without either wait for capacity, or — more often — get answered anyway from raw and partially-modeled data that nobody has validated. That second path is the expensive one: it produces decisions made on poor-quality information, and it does so invisibly, because the answer looks like every other answer. As new product areas launch faster than coverage can follow, the share of the business sitting in that category grows.
2.  The standards are conventions, not policy. They are real and consistently applied, but they are not written down as organizational commitments with owners and review. Growth is what converts this from a tolerable risk into a certainty.
3.  The forward constraint is the binding one. Agent-accessible data, fleet expansion analytics, and squad self-service all require modeled coverage in domains that don't have it, plus semantic metadata that nothing currently produces. These are capabilities Runpod doesn't have yet — not risks it's carrying — and the bar rises with growth: more squads needing self-service, more fleet/users to reason about, more surface area for agents to work across.
4.  The volume arrives whether or not the team exists. Runpod is entering a phase of rapid growth, with new product squads and new datasets emerging faster than at any prior point. As Brennen mentioned in our last Engineering retrospective, “one of the reasons Runpod has been able to do so well is because of our data. (going forward) making sure we feed into this system (event stream) will be required”. Review and modeling demand scales with squad count and dataset count. Review supply is currently one person doing it voluntarily, because they believe it matters — not because the organization has assigned it to anyone. That is not a capacity gap; it is a function with no owner, about to meet a step change in load.

Growth is the common thread. The third point is the reason to act. The fourth is the reason to act now: the window to build this cheaply is closing, because the datasets are coming either way. They will land shaped or unshaped, and reshaping them later costs migrations, backfills, and inconsistent data. The first two explain why acting now is cheap — there is no cleanup phase. The work is extension and formalization of a model that already works.

## Structure and naming

### The umbrella

Runpod today has a single Data team containing Data Analytics, Data Engineering, and Data Science, though the distinction between Data Analytics and Data Science is not currently well defined. This proposal resolves that ambiguity by establishing a Data Science discipline with three distinct teams:

Data Science (discipline)

├── Decision Science ← today's Data Analytics team, rechartered

├── Product Data Science ← new team

└── Data Platform Engineering ← today's Data Engineering members

### Why these names

|  |  |
| :-: | :-: |
| Team | Named for |

# Abstract

Environments can change in incremental fashions, where a shift from one state to another occurs over multiple organismal generations. The rate at which the environment changes is expected to influence how and how well populations adapt to the ultimate environment. We use a model system, the lytic RNA bacteriophage Φ6, to investigate this question empirically. We evolved viruses for thermostability by exposing them to heat shocks that increased to a maximum temperature at different rates. We observed increases in the ability of most heat-shocked populations to survive high temperature heat shocks. However, neither the survival of endpoint populations at the highest temperature heat shock nor the number of mutations per population varied significantly according to the rate of thermal change. We also evaluated mutations from the endpoint populations for their effects on viral thermostability and growth. As expected, some of the mutations studied increased viral thermostability. However, other mutations decreased thermostability but increased growth rate, suggesting that viruses still experienced selection for replication. Our study highlights the importance of considering the effects of multiple selective pressures, even in environments where a single factor is changing.

# Abstract

Environments can change in incremental fashions, where a shift from one state to another occurs over multiple organismal generations. The rate at which the environment changes is expected to influence how and how well populations adapt to the ultimate environment. We use a model system, the lytic RNA bacteriophage Φ6, to investigate this question empirically. We evolved viruses for thermostability by exposing them to heat shocks that increased to a maximum temperature at different rates. We observed increases in the ability of most heat-shocked populations to survive high temperature heat shocks. However, neither the survival of endpoint populations at the highest temperature heat shock nor the number of mutations per population varied significantly according to the rate of thermal change. We also evaluated mutations from the endpoint populations for their effects on viral thermostability and growth. As expected, some of the mutations studied increased viral thermostability. However, other mutations decreased thermostability but increased growth rate, suggesting that viruses still experienced selection for replication. Our study highlights the importance of considering the effects of multiple selective pressures, even in environments where a single factor is changing.

## What this document is for

Over the last 18 months, Runpod has built a world-class medallion architecture, tools for quickly adding new data sets to it, and a number of high-quality gold data products that can be effectively used throughout the organization.

| Re-embed existing Data team ICs | Same recall problem, plus a different mandate: Data Analytics is chartered to answer questions, and this role is chartered to make squads able to answer their own. One team holding both means the urgent job wins every time. |
| Matrix / dotted line into squads | Addresses presence but not incentives or the review norm. A reviewer accountable elsewhere signs off to whatever depth the deadline allows. |
| Do nothing until we're larger | The cost of getting grain and identifiers right is near zero at design time and enormous afterward. The datasets are arriving either way; they land shaped or unshaped. Reshaping later means migrations and backfills that are rarely possible. |

### If two hires is not available now

Phase 0 is the charter plus the Data Design Review, staffed by me, no new headcount, for one quarter — with rework rate on reviewed versus unreviewed data surfaces reported at the end. Phase 1 is the hires, triggered by \[squad count / new event stream rate / Phase 0 rework data\].

This is a real fallback, not a preferred option. Phase 0 without a committed trigger for Phase 1 is the status quo with a name on it, and the coverage gap it leaves is described under Staffing.

## What this costs us today

\[Lead with the serverless metrics case. Recommended shape:\]

We shipped serverless throttling and cold start time instrumentation without a design-time review of grain and identifiers. Correcting it required \[what it required\]. It cost \[engineer-weeks / decisions made on unreliable numbers / how long the metric was untrustworthy\]. The design-time conversation that would have prevented it was \[a 30-minute discussion / a single field\].

\[One or two more instances if available. Then:\]

Domains with modeled, curated coverage get fast and trustworthy answers. Domains without it wait for capacity or — more often — get answered anyway from raw data that has not been validated and is not optimized for analytical use. That second path produces decisions made on poor-quality information using undefined methodologies, and it does so invisibly.

As Brennen noted in our last Engineering retrospective: "one of the reasons Runpod has been able to do so well is because of our data. \[Going forward\] making sure we feed into this system \[event stream\] will be required."

[Assaying fitness](#h.5kvp31s52nod)

[References](#h.cgg9hmb4ztk7)

# Abstract

Environments can change in incremental fashions, where a shift from one state to another occurs over multiple organismal generations. The rate at which the environment changes is expected to influence how and how well populations adapt to the ultimate environment. We use a model system, the lytic RNA bacteriophage Φ6, to investigate this question empirically. We evolved viruses for thermostability by exposing them to heat shocks that increased to a maximum temperature at different rates. We observed increases in the ability of most heat-shocked populations to survive high temperature heat shocks. However, neither the survival of endpoint populations at the highest temperature heat shock nor the number of mutations per population varied significantly according to the rate of thermal change. We also evaluated mutations from the endpoint populations for their effects on viral thermostability and growth. As expected, some of the mutations studied increased viral thermostability. However, other mutations decreased thermostability but increased growth rate, suggesting that viruses still experienced selection for replication. Our study highlights the importance of considering the effects of multiple selective pressures, even in environments where a single factor is changing.

# Introduction

The process of de novo adaptation is typically studied in the context of the simplest form of environmental change, an abrupt shift from an old environmental state to a new one (e.g., Orr 1998). Immediately following the environmental change, the mean fitness of the population shifts to a relatively low value (that is, it is poorly adapted to that environment). The population’s mean fitness then increases as the population gains and fixes beneficial mutations. Under Fisher’s geometric model, the population is expected first to fix mutations that confer large gains in fitness, followed by mutations of increasingly smaller beneficial effect as the population approaches the optimal phenotype of environment (Orr 1998).

However, natural environments rarely change abruptly to a new constant state. Rather, environmental changes can occur more gradually, on scales that encompass multiple organismal generations. For example, shifts between glacial and interglacial periods occurred over thousands of years (Davis 1981; Davis and Shaw 2001; Davis et al. 2005). Even changes that are rapid on geological scales, such as anthropogenic climate change (e.g., Keeling et al. 1995) or changes in pollution levels (e.g., Warneke et al. 2012), occur over multiple decades. Adaptation may proceed very differently in such cases of incremental environmental change (Bello & Waxman 2006, Kopp & Hermisson 2007, Collins 2007).

Evolution in an incrementally changing environment is often modeled using a quantitative genetic framework. In the simplest cases, a single quantitative trait evolves with Gaussian stabilizing selection under conditions where the optimal phenotype is constantly shifting (Lynch et al. 1991, Lynch & Lande 1993, Bürger & Lynch 1995, Bello & Waxman 2006, Kopp & Hermisson 2007, Gomulkiewicz & Houle 2009, Kopp & Matuszewski 2014). 1	# Investigation Ledger Templates
2	
3	Create the ledger at Plan time, before any planned data is collected.
4	Create means write: the ledger exists as a file before the first planned collection runs, so the preregistration leaves a record the transcript can verify — a ledger first materialized in the final report is a reconstruction, not a preregistration.
5	Keep it in scratch space by default, named recognizably (e.g. `ledger.md`); put it in the project directory when the user wants a durable artifact.
6	The ledger is append-only where integrity matters: preregistered predictions and amendment entries are immutable once written.
7	A test entry's outcome and evidence fields are the only sanctioned in-place updates: they transition once from `NOT_TESTED` to a terminal value when the test runs, and any later revision requires a dated amendment instead of an edit.
8	
9	## Full Route Template
10	
11	```markdown
12	# Investigation: <one-line question>
13	
14	## Problem
15	
16	- Decision informed: <what will be done differently depending on the answer>
17	- Falsifiable question: <the question, scoped to population, timeframe, units>
18	- Success criteria: answered means <observable condition>
19	- Stop condition: <precommitted criterion for concluding or stopping>
20	- Effort budget: <tool calls | queries | wall-clock — pick one and a number>
21	
22	## Hypotheses
23	
24	| id | claim | Candidate explanation | Prediction if true | Prediction if false | Necessary prediction (failure refutes) | Cheapest adequate test | Data needed |
25	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
26	| H1 | causal | ... | ... | ... | ... | T1 | ... |
27	| H2 | descriptive (estimand: ...) | ... | ... | ... | ... | T2 | ... |
28	
29	The necessary-prediction column is what makes status mechanically derivable: declare it at Plan time, before any outcome is read.
30	Every row must carry one.
31	What a necessary prediction must be able to do, the scope at which refutation acts, and the disposition of a row whose prediction cannot fail are governed by SKILL.md's Plan and Conclusion sections, the single authority; read them there rather than from any summary here.
32	Each row declares its claim as `causal`, `descriptive`, or `data-artifact`, and a descriptive row names the estimand its prediction is about.
33	A `data-artifact` row claims the records themselves are wrong — missing, miscounted, mis-instrumented.
34	The claim column is what the status rules read, and those rules — including what each class can and cannot be `REFUTED` by — live in SKILL.md's Conclusion section, which is the single authority.
35	Read them there; this template deliberately does not summarize them, because a rule kept in two places is how the disposition of a faulted worker return drifted into a contradiction (issue #103).
36	
37	Hypotheses added after seeing data get the label `retrospective` in the id column (e.g. `H4 (retrospective)`).
38	The bar a retrospective hypothesis must clear to be promoted lives in SKILL.md's Conclusion section, the single authority; read it there rather than from any summary here.
39	Inspecting inventory, schemas, provenance, and coverage does not make a hypothesis retrospective; inspecting a cause-outcome relationship does.
40	
41	## Sources
42	
43	| id | Origin (file, query, system) | Acquired | Coverage notes |
44	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
45	| S1 | ... | ... | ... |
46	
47	Every evidence cell in Tests references a source id, so results stay reproducible against the exact data used.
48	
49	## Data Validity
50	
51	- Collection method: <how each source is produced>
52	- Coverage matrix: <row counts at the crossed grain the analysis uses — every time bucket compared × every segment appearing in a denominator, contrast, or hypothesis. Separate per-period and per-segment totals do not substitute: a hole in one segment on a few days hides between them.>
53	- Field population: <the populated rate of each field relied on, at that same crossed grain; a field present for only part of the data is a coverage gap, not a null problem>
54	- Coverage baseline: <the expected schedule or independent denominator the matrix was compared against; if neither exists, record coverage as unverifiable rather than clean>
55	- Known instrument failures: <dashboards, exporters, sampling quirks>
56	- Source completeness semantics: <per source whose absent records bear on any conclusion: what an absent record means — event absent, event unrecorded, or export incomplete — and the evidence for that reading; `UNKNOWN` when no evidence exists or the evidence does not discriminate between the live readings — the source's own missingness pattern never does — which blocks inferring event status or any directional missingness claim from that source's absent records>
57	A source declared `UNKNOWN` is written in the machine-checkable per-source form `<source-id>: UNKNOWN — <why no evidence discriminates the live readings>`, one declaration per source, so a scorer can confirm the declaration without judging the prose.
58	- Sensitivity checks performed: <intervals computed and known positives surfaced — fresh draws per trial or independent data, never intervals recomputed from one fixed shifted copy — plus detection limits>
59	
60	## Tests
61	
62	| id | Hypothesis | Preregistered prediction | Method | Outcome | Evidence |
63	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
64	| T1 | H1 | ... | ... | NOT_TESTED | S1 ... |
65	
66	One row per test-hypothesis pair: a test that bears on several hypotheses gets one row each, because a discriminating observation can be `CONSISTENT` for one hypothesis and `CONTRADICTED` for another.
67	Outcomes: `NOT_TESTED` → `CONSISTENT` / `CONTRADICTED` / `NON_DISCRIMINATING`.
68	A `NON_DISCRIMINATING` outcome states why (underpowered, wrong grain, no known-positive check available) and any detection limit.
69	A `CONTRADICTED` outcome that refutes on a positive or distributional contradiction — an observed pattern, timing, or count offered as failing a distributional prediction — records the adequacy bound the skill requires (SKILL.md, Data) beside the outcome, in the machine-checkable form `adequacy: <rate> ± <uncertainty> (variants: <range>)`.
70	Record it in that row's `Outcome` or `Evidence` cell, or in the hypothesis's Conclusion `basis` cell — both are accepted sites — and note that the machine check requires a rate and a variant range, treating the `± <uncertainty>` part as optional, so stating the uncertainty remains a matter of the skill's rule rather than the checker's.
71	A deterministic prediction a true instance could never fail is exempt and records no bound.
72	
73	## Amendments
74	
75	- <date>: <what changed and why — new data request, new hypothesis, revised budget>
76	- <date>: T<id> outcome superseded: <old> → <new>, because <reason — e.g. unit error found during spot-verification>
77	
78	An amendment that supersedes a test outcome names the test id, the replacement outcome, and the reason; hypothesis status derives from each test's latest effective outcome.
79	
80	## Conclusion
81	
82	- Answer: <answer first>
83	- Best supported: <explanation(s), with the discriminating evidence>
84	- Per-hypothesis summary — `status` is `REFUTED` or `UNRESOLVED` and nothing else:
85	
86	  | id | claim | status | basis |
87	  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
88	  | H1 | causal | UNRESOLVED | <the discriminating evidence, or why nothing settled it> |
89	
90	  "Best supported" is conclusion language, not a status: it belongs in `basis`, as the worked example shows.
91	- Limitations: <named unresolved alternatives, data gaps, associative-only claims>
92	```
93	
94	## Mini Route Template
95	
96	One paragraph, inline in the conversation or scratch space:
97	
98	```markdown
99	Claim: <the single stated claim>.
100	Prediction: <what I expect to observe if it holds / if it fails>.
101	Probe(s): <the bounded read-only probes that settle it — as many as it takes; a probe count is a budget, not a hypothesis>.
102	Stop condition: <what makes the claim settled, or settles that this data cannot settle it>.
103	Outcome: <CONSISTENT / CONTRADICTED / NON_DISCRIMINATING, with evidence pointer>.
104	Answer: <conclusion, with any limitation>.
105	```
106	
107	## Costly Collection Plan Template
108	
109	Written before any costly pull, on whatever route selected it — including `direct`.
110	It adds no hypotheses; on the full route these fields are already carried by Problem and Plan, so do not duplicate them.
111	
112	```markdown
113	Serves: <the decision or output this pull is for>.
114	Source and action: <the exact system, query, or endpoint, and what is run against it>.
115	Cheapest adequate: <why this pull, and not a cheaper one, is the least that answers it>.
116	Budget: <maximum spend in the metered unit — queries, rows, dollars, wall-clock>.
117	Already paid for: <data already pulled that this plan reuses — what, at what grain and snapshot, and its spend counted against the budget — or none>.
118	Authorization: <the grant covering this action, per the authorization gate — or BLOCKED, and what is needed>.
119	Stop / re-pull condition: <what would make this enough, and what would justify paying again>.
120	```
121	
122	## Estimation Route Template
123	
124	```markdown
125	Goal: <the knowledge goal or decision the estimate informs>.
126	Estimand: <the quantity being estimated, precisely defined>.
127	Population: <who or what the estimate describes, over what period>.
128	Uncertainty method: <interval, resampling, or stated inability to quantify>.
129	Practical threshold: <the value at which the decision changes>.
130	Stop condition: <what makes the estimate good enough, or settles that this data cannot tighten it further>.
131	Result: <estimate with uncertainty, compared against the threshold>.
132	Limitations: <coverage gaps, selection concerns, associative-only caveats>.
133	```
134	
135	## Worked Example (full route, abridged)
136	
137	```markdown
138	# Investigation: API p95 latency doubled on Tue 2026-07-07 — why?
139	
140	## Problem
141	
142	- Decision informed: roll back the Tuesday deploy, or leave it and fix elsewhere.
143	- Falsifiable question: what explains the p95 latency increase for /checkout between 2026-07-06 and 2026-07-08 (ms, per-request, US region)?
144	- Success criteria: answered means one or more explanations account for the observed increase and survive a discriminating test.
145	- Stop condition: conclude when no named unresolved alternative could reverse the rollback decision.
146	- Effort budget: 25 queries.
147	
148	## Hypotheses
149	
150	| id | claim | Candidate explanation | Prediction if true | Prediction if false | Necessary prediction (failure refutes) | Cheapest adequate test | Data needed |
151	| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
152	| H1 | causal | Tuesday deploy regressed the cache layer, causing the observed p95 step | p95 step aligns with deploy timestamp; cache hit rate drops | p95 shift precedes deploy or hit rate flat | the p95 step must not precede the deploy — a deploy cannot cause a step that happened before it | T1 | deploy log, cache metrics |
153	| H2 | causal | Traffic mix shifted toward uncached endpoints | share of cache-miss routes rises independently of deploy | route mix stable across the step | the cache-miss route share must rise at the step | T2 | request logs by route |
154	| H3 | descriptive (estimand: cache-miss route share on the new client version minus cache-miss route share on the old, 2026-07-06 to 2026-07-08) | Cache-miss route traffic is concentrated on the new client version | cache-miss route traffic concentrates in one client version | cache-miss route traffic is spread evenly across versions | the cache-miss route share must be higher on the new client version than on the old | T3 | request logs by user agent |
155	| H4 (retrospective) | causal | Upstream payment API slowdown drives most of the added latency | /checkout spans show payment call dominating added latency | added latency spread across spans | the payment span must account for the majority of added p95 — "drives most of" is false otherwise | T4 | trace spans |
156	| H5 | data-artifact | The 07-07 21:00–23:00 `/checkout` log shortfall is a logging-pipeline gap, not a traffic drop | an independent request counter shows normal traffic in that window | the independent counter also shows a dip | the load balancer's counter must not dip when the logs do | T6 | LB request counter |
157	
158	## Sources
159	
160	| id | Origin (file, query, system) | Acquired | Coverage notes |
161	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
162	| S1 | deploy log `deploys/2026-07-07.log` | 2026-07-08 09:00Z | full day |
163	| S2 | cache metrics dashboard export, 5-min grain | 2026-07-08 09:05Z | 10% request sample |
164	| S3 | raw request logs `logs/checkout-2026-07-0{6,7,8}.jsonl.gz` | 2026-07-08 09:10Z | all rows; user-agent field populated for only ~30% of rows |
165	| S4 | trace spans, Jaeger query `/checkout` 07-06..07-08 | 2026-07-08 10:40Z | 1% trace sampling |
166	| S5 | load balancer request counter, 1-hour grain | 2026-07-08 11:15Z | independent of the logging pipeline — used as the coverage baseline |
167	
168	## Data Validity
169	
170	- Collection method: dashboard aggregates from the metrics pipeline; raw request logs and traces available.
171	- Coverage matrix: the analysis compares hours × route, so request-log rows were counted at that grain across 07-06..07-08. Every hour carries 3.9k–4.4k rows on every route, except `/checkout` on 07-07 21:00–23:00, which carries ~1.2k/hour — a shortfall confined to one route and three hours. Per-day totals (11.9M, 11.7M, 11.8M) and per-route totals both look healthy and would have hidden it, which is exactly why they are not the check.
172	- Field population: at the same hour × route grain, `route` and `latency_ms` are 100% populated throughout; `user_agent` is populated for ~30% of rows overall and drops to ~4% on mobile routes after 07-07 12:00 — a coverage gap, not a null problem, and the reason T3 below cannot discriminate.
173	- Coverage matrix, trace spans (S4): H4/T4 contrasts payment spans against other spans, so span type is a segment the analysis uses and needs its own matrix at hour × span-type. Every hour carries 40–70 sampled traces per span type across both days, with `span_name` and `duration_ms` 100% populated — no hole, so T4's span breakdown rests on checked coverage rather than on S4's global "1% sampling" note, which describes the sample rate and says nothing about whether the sample is evenly spread.
174	- Coverage baseline: compared against the load balancer's independent request counter, which shows no dip in the 07-07 21:00–23:00 window — so the shortfall is in the logging pipeline, not in real traffic. Promoted to H5 (see Amendments) rather than analyzed as a traffic change.
175	- Known instrument failures: dashboard p95 is computed over 5-minute windows and hides sub-window spikes.
176	- Source completeness semantics: S3 request logs — an absent row means the logging pipeline dropped it, not that no request occurred (established by the independent LB counter, S5/T6); S2 dashboard export and S4 trace spans — designed samples (10% and 1%, stated in Sources), so absence means unsampled by design.
177	S1: UNKNOWN — no completeness contract checked, so no conclusion infers event status or bias direction from its absence.
178	S5: UNKNOWN — same.
179	- Sensitivity checks performed: dashboard step cross-checked against raw logs (known positive: the step appears in both), so the dashboard is not blind to steps of this size.
180	
181	## Tests
182	
183	| id | Hypothesis | Preregistered prediction | Method | Outcome | Evidence |

# Investigation Ledger Templates

Create the ledger at Plan time, before any planned data is collected.
Create means write: the ledger exists as a file before the first planned collection runs, so the preregistration leaves a record the transcript can verify — a ledger first materialized in the final report is a reconstruction, not a preregistration.
Keep it in scratch space by default, named recognizably (e.g. `ledger.md`); put it in the project directory when the user wants a durable artifact.
The ledger is append-only where integrity matters: preregistered predictions and amendment entries are immutable once written.
A test entry's outcome and evidence fields are the only sanctioned in-place updates: they transition once from `NOT_TESTED` to a terminal value when the test runs, and any later revision requires a dated amendment instead of an edit.

## Full Route Template

```markdown
# Investigation: <one-line question>

## Problem

- Decision informed: <what will be done differently depending on the answer>
- Falsifiable question: <the question, scoped to population, timeframe, units>
- Success criteria: answered means <observable condition>
- Stop condition: <precommitted criterion for concluding or stopping>
- Effort budget: <tool calls | queries | wall-clock — pick one and a number>

## Hypotheses

| id | claim | Candidate explanation | Prediction if true | Prediction if false | Necessary prediction (failure refutes) | Cheapest adequate test | Data needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H1 | causal | ... | ... | ... | ... | T1 | ... |
| H2 | descriptive (estimand: ...) | ... | ... | ... | ... | T2 | ... |

The necessary-prediction column is what makes status mechanically derivable: declare it at Plan time, before any outcome is read.
Every row must carry one.
What a necessary prediction must be able to do, the scope at which refutation acts, and the disposition of a row whose prediction cannot fail are governed by SKILL.md's Plan and Conclusion sections, the single authority; read them there rather than from any summary here.
Each row declares its claim as `causal`, `descriptive`, or `data-artifact`, and a descriptive row names the estimand its prediction is about.
A `data-artifact` row claims the records themselves are wrong — missing, miscounted, mis-instrumented.
The claim column is what the status rules read, and those rules — including what each class can and cannot be `REFUTED` by — live in SKILL.md's Conclusion section, which is the single authority.
Read them there; this template deliberately does not summarize them, because a rule kept in two places is how the disposition of a faulted worker return drifted into a contradiction (issue #103).

Hypotheses added after seeing data get the label `retrospective` in the id column (e.g. `H4 (retrospective)`).
The bar a retrospective hypothesis must clear to be promoted lives in SKILL.md's Conclusion section, the single authority; read it there rather than from any summary here.
Inspecting inventory, schemas, provenance, and coverage does not make a hypothesis retrospective; inspecting a cause-outcome relationship does.

## Sources

| id | Origin (file, query, system) | Acquired | Coverage notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | ... | ... | ... |

Every evidence cell in Tests references a source id, so results stay reproducible against the exact data used.

## Data Validity

- Collection method: <how each source is produced>
- Coverage matrix: <row counts at the crossed grain the analysis uses — every time bucket compared × every segment appearing in a denominator, contrast, or hypothesis. Separate per-period and per-segment totals do not substitute: a hole in one segment on a few days hides between them.>
- Field population: <the populated rate of each field relied on, at that same crossed grain; a field present for only part of the data is a coverage gap, not a null problem>
- Coverage baseline: <the expected schedule or independent denominator the matrix was compared against; if neither exists, record coverage as unverifiable rather than clean>
- Known instrument failures: <dashboards, exporters, sampling quirks>
- Source completeness semantics: <per source whose absent records bear on any conclusion: what an absent record means — event absent, event unrecorded, or export incomplete — and the evidence for that reading; `UNKNOWN` when no evidence exists or the evidence does not discriminate between the live readings — the source's own missingness pattern never does — which blocks inferring event status or any directional missingness claim from that source's absent records>
A source declared `UNKNOWN` is written in the machine-checkable per-source form `<source-id>: UNKNOWN — <why no evidence discriminates the live readings>`, one declaration per source, so a scorer can confirm the declaration without judging the prose.
- Sensitivity checks performed: <intervals computed and known positives surfaced — fresh draws per trial or independent data, never intervals recomputed from one fixed shifted copy — plus detection limits>

## Tests

| id | Hypothesis | Preregistered prediction | Method | Outcome | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | H1 | ... | ... | NOT_TESTED | S1 ... |

One row per test-hypothesis pair: a test that bears on several hypotheses gets one row each, because a discriminating observation can be `CONSISTENT` for one hypothesis and `CONTRADICTED` for another.
Outcomes: `NOT_TESTED` → `CONSISTENT` / `CONTRADICTED` / `NON_DISCRIMINATING`.
A `NON_DISCRIMINATING` outcome states why (underpowered, wrong grain, no known-positive check available) and any detection limit.
A `CONTRADICTED` outcome that refutes on a positive or distributional contradiction — an observed pattern, timing, or count offered as failing a distributional prediction — records the adequacy bound the skill requires (SKILL.md, Data) beside the outcome, in the machine-checkable form `adequacy: <rate> ± <uncertainty> (variants: <range>)`.
Record it in that row's `Outcome` or `Evidence` cell, or in the hypothesis's Conclusion `basis` cell — both are accepted sites — and note that the machine check requires a rate and a variant range, treating the `± <uncertainty>` part as optional, so stating the uncertainty remains a matter of the skill's rule rather than the checker's.
A deterministic prediction a true instance could never fail is exempt and records no bound.

## Amendments

- <date>: <what changed and why — new data request, new hypothesis, revised budget>
- <date>: T<id> outcome superseded: <old> → <new>, because <reason — e.g. unit error found during spot-verification>

An amendment that supersedes a test outcome names the test id, the replacement outcome, and the reason; hypothesis status derives from each test's latest effective outcome.

## Conclusion

- Answer: <answer first>
- Best supported: <explanation(s), with the discriminating evidence>
- Per-hypothesis summary — `status` is `REFUTED` or `UNRESOLVED` and nothing else:

  | id | claim | status | basis |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | H1 | causal | UNRESOLVED | <the discriminating evidence, or why nothing settled it> |

  "Best supported" is conclusion language, not a status: it belongs in `basis`, as the worked example shows.
- Limitations: <named unresolved alternatives, data gaps, associative-only claims>
```

## Mini Route Template

One paragraph, inline in the conversation or scratch space:

```markdown
Claim: <the single stated claim>.
Prediction: <what I expect to observe if it holds / if it fails>.
Probe(s): <the bounded read-only probes that settle it — as many as it takes; a probe count is a budget, not a hypothesis>.
Stop condition: <what makes the claim settled, or settles that this data cannot settle it>.
Outcome: <CONSISTENT / CONTRADICTED / NON_DISCRIMINATING, with evidence pointer>.
Answer: <conclusion, with any limitation>.
```

## Costly Collection Plan Template

Written before any costly pull, on whatever route selected it — including `direct`.
It adds no hypotheses; on the full route these fields are already carried by Problem and Plan, so do not duplicate them.

```markdown
Serves: <the decision or output this pull is for>.
Source and action: <the exact system, query, or endpoint, and what is run against it>.
Cheapest adequate: <why this pull, and not a cheaper one, is the least that answers it>.
Budget: <maximum spend in the metered unit — queries, rows, dollars, wall-clock>.
Already paid for: <data already pulled that this plan reuses — what, at what grain and snapshot, and its spend counted against the budget — or none>.
Authorization: <the grant covering this action, per the authorization gate — or BLOCKED, and what is needed>.
Stop / re-pull condition: <what would make this enough, and what would justify paying again>.
```

## Estimation Route Template

```markdown
Goal: <the knowledge goal or decision the estimate informs>.
Estimand: <the quantity being estimated, precisely defined>.
Population: <who or what the estimate describes, over what period>.
Uncertainty method: <interval, resampling, or stated inability to quantify>.
Practical threshold: <the value at which the decision changes>.
Stop condition: <what makes the estimate good enough, or settles that this data cannot tighten it further>.
Result: <estimate with uncertainty, compared against the threshold>.
Limitations: <coverage gaps, selection concerns, associative-only caveats>.
```

## Worked Example (full route, abridged)

# Investigation: API p95 latency doubled on Tue 2026-07-07 — why?

## Problem

- Decision informed: roll back the Tuesday deploy, or leave it and fix elsewhere.
- Falsifiable question: what explains the p95 latency increase for /checkout between 2026-07-06 and 2026-07-08 (ms, per-request, US region)?
- Success criteria: answered means one or more explanations account for the observed increase and survive a discriminating test.
- Stop condition: conclude when no named unresolved alternative could reverse the rollback decision.
- Effort budget: 25 queries.

## Hypotheses

| id | claim | Candidate explanation | Prediction if true | Prediction if false | Necessary prediction (failure refutes) | Cheapest adequate test | Data needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| H2 | causal | Traffic mix shifted toward uncached endpoints | share of cache-miss routes rises independently of deploy | route mix stable across the step | the cache-miss route share must rise at the step | T2 | request logs by route |
| H3 | descriptive (estimand: cache-miss route share on the new client version minus cache-miss route share on the old, 2026-07-06 to 2026-07-08) | Cache-miss route traffic is concentrated on the new client version | cache-miss route traffic concentrates in one client version | cache-miss route traffic is spread evenly across versions | the cache-miss route share must be higher on the new client version than on the old | T3 | request logs by user agent |
| H4 (retrospective) | causal | Upstream payment API slowdown drives most of the added latency | /checkout spans show payment call dominating added latency | added latency spread across spans | the payment span must account for the majority of added p95 — "drives most of" is false otherwise | T4 | trace spans |
| H5 | data-artifact | The 07-07 21:00–23:00 `/checkout` log shortfall is a logging-pipeline gap, not a traffic drop | an independent request counter shows normal traffic in that window | the independent counter also shows a dip | the load balancer's counter must not dip when the logs do | T6 | LB request counter |

## Sources

| id | Origin (file, query, system) | Acquired | Coverage notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | deploy log `deploys/2026-07-07.log` | 2026-07-08 09:00Z | full day |
| S2 | cache metrics dashboard export, 5-min grain | 2026-07-08 09:05Z | 10% request sample |
| S3 | raw request logs `logs/checkout-2026-07-0{6,7,8}.jsonl.gz` | 2026-07-08 09:10Z | all rows; user-agent field populated for only ~30% of rows |
| S4 | trace spans, Jaeger query `/checkout` 07-06..07-08 | 2026-07-08 10:40Z | 1% trace sampling |
| S5 | load balancer request counter, 1-hour grain | 2026-07-08 11:15Z | independent of the logging pipeline — used as the coverage baseline |

Per-day totals (11.9M, 11.7M, 11.8M) and per-route totals both look healthy and would have hidden it, which is exactly why they are not the check.
- Field population: at the same hour × route grain, `route` and `latency_ms` are 100% populated throughout; `user_agent` is populated for ~30% of rows overall and drops to ~4% on mobile routes after 07-07 12:00 — a coverage gap, not a null problem, and the reason T3 below cannot discriminate.
- Coverage matrix, trace spans (S4): H4/T4 contrasts payment spans against other spans, so span type is a segment the analysis uses and needs its own matrix at hour × span-type. Every hour carries 40–70 sampled traces per span type across both days, with `span_name` and `duration_ms` 100% populated — no hole, so T4's span breakdown rests on checked coverage rather than on S4's global "1% sampling" note, which describes the sample rate and says nothing about whether the sample is evenly spread.
- Coverage baseline: compared against the load balancer's independent request counter, which shows no dip in the 07-07 21:00–23:00 window — so the shortfall is in the logging pipeline, not in real traffic. Promoted to H5 (see Amendments) rather than analyzed as a traffic change.
- Known instrument failures: dashboard p95 is computed over 5-minute windows and hides sub-window spikes.
- Source completeness semantics: S3 request logs — an absent row means the logging pipeline dropped it, not that no request occurred (established by the independent LB counter, S5/T6); S2 dashboard export and S4 trace spans — designed samples (10% and 1%, stated in Sources), so absence means unsampled by design.
S1: UNKNOWN — no completeness contract checked, so no conclusion infers event status or bias direction from its absence.
S5: UNKNOWN — same.
- Sensitivity checks performed: dashboard step cross-checked against raw logs (known positive: the step appears in both), so the dashboard is not blind to steps of this size.

| id | Hypothesis | Preregistered prediction | Method | Outcome | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | H1 | the p95 step does not precede the deploy | align deploy log with metrics | CONTRADICTED | step at 09:12, deploy at 14:30 — the step precedes the deploy by over five hours (S1, S2 §3) |

| T2 | H2 | cache-miss route share rises ≥10pp at the step | group logs by route across the step | CONSISTENT | cache-miss route share 22%→41% at 09:10 (S3 §4) |
| T3 | H3 | cache-miss route share higher on the new client version than on the old | group cache-miss route traffic by user agent | NON_DISCRIMINATING | user-agent populated for only ~30% of rows (Sources S3); cannot detect a shift smaller than ~25pp (S3 §5) |

# Investigation: Why did the Northgate Clinic account's spend drop last quarter?

Status: **BLOCKED at Data.** Plan preregistered 2026-08-11 before any collection. No test has run.

## Problem

- Decision informed: whether to treat Northgate Clinic as an at-risk account needing
  intervention (save motion, pricing review) or as a measurement/timing artifact needing none.
- Falsifiable question: what accounts for the decrease in Northgate Clinic's spend
  between the prior quarter and last quarter? Population, timeframe, and units are
  **unpinned** — see Open Questions; "spend" (billed revenue vs. usage vs. bookings),
  the quarter boundaries, and the fiscal calendar are all unstated.
- Success criteria: answered means one or more explanations account for the observed
  decrease in magnitude, and survive a test that discriminates them from the rivals below.
- Stop condition: conclude when no named unresolved alternative could reverse the
  at-risk determination; stop with limits if the source cannot separate rate from volume.
- Effort budget: 25 queries once a source is authorized.

## Hypotheses (preregistered before any data was seen)

Framed from the shape of the question alone. No cause–outcome relationship has been
inspected, so none of these is `retrospective`.

| id | claim | Candidate explanation | Prediction if true | Prediction if false | Necessary prediction (failure refutes) | Cheapest adequate test | Data needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H1 | data-artifact | The drop is a definitional/calendar effect, not a change in the account — shifted quarter boundary, a billing run landing outside the window, or a changed fiscal calendar | Re-cutting spend on equal-length calendar windows removes most of the gap; a billing event sits just outside the boundary | The gap survives re-cutting on equal windows | Re-cut on equal-length windows must remove the majority of the gap | Re-aggregate the same transactions on aligned windows | Transaction-level spend with dates |
| H2 | descriptive (estimand: last-quarter volume minus prior-quarter volume, in billable units) | Volume fell — the clinic bought/used less at an unchanged rate | Billable units drop proportionally to spend; effective rate flat | Units flat or up while spend falls | Billable units must fall | Decompose spend into units × effective rate | Units and spend per period |
| H3 | descriptive (estimand: last-quarter effective rate minus prior-quarter effective rate, per billable unit) | Rate fell — discount, renegotiated contract, plan downgrade, or credit/refund applied | Effective rate drops; units roughly flat | Effective rate flat | Effective rate must fall | Same decomposition as H2, read on the rate factor | Units, spend, contract/discount records |
| H4 | descriptive (estimand: share of spend by line-of-business/site/product, both quarters) | Composition shifted — one site, product line, or service stopped while others held | The drop concentrates in a small number of components; others flat | The drop is spread evenly across all components | The drop must concentrate rather than be uniform | Break the delta down by component and rank contributions | Spend by component |
| H5 | causal | The spend moved rather than stopped — same activity displaced to a sibling account, a new contract entity, a reseller, or a different billing ID | A sibling/related account shows an offsetting increase in the same period | No related account absorbs the volume | An offsetting increase must appear somewhere in the account family | Look up related accounts on the same parent/entity and sum across the family | Account hierarchy + spend for related accounts |

Notes on the field: H1, H4, and H5 are the rivals a narrow "why did this customer
churn?" framing routinely omits — a framing effect, a composition shift, and the same
activity displaced outside the measured slice. H2/H3 are the two factors of the moved
total; testing only one attributes the residual to the other without a test, which is
the confirmation this loop exists to prevent.

Not in the table, deliberately: "demand fell / the customer is unhappy" is the residual,
not a hypothesis. If H1–H5 leave a gap unexplained, that gap is reported as
**unattributed**, not renamed as churn risk.

## Sources

| id | Origin (file, query, system) | Acquired | Coverage notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| — | none | — | No source located or authorized |

Orientation performed (read-only, cheap, no cause–outcome relationship inspected):

- Working directory and the whole session scratchpad tree: no billing, CRM, or spend data.
  The only `Northgate` matches are transcripts of this same prompt from prior runs of
  this eval harness — not data, and not evidence.
- Connected MCP servers: weather (Tempest), network quality (Orb/Orbnet), IP geolocation,
  Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive. None is a billing, CRM, or revenue system.
- Google Drive full-text search for `Northgate`: no relevant file (one spurious match on
  the phrase "spend a rainy Sunday").

Instrument check (per the rule that a negative result needs a known positive before it is
trusted): both search instruments were confirmed able to surface a positive. `grep -ril`
over the same tree returned hits for a control term; Drive `fullText contains 'spend'`
returned real documents. The empty `Northgate` results are therefore an absence of data,
not a broken search.

## Data Validity

- Collection method: n/a — no source reached.
- Coverage matrix: not built. It cannot be built without a source.
- Source completeness semantics: n/a — no source declared.
- Sensitivity checks performed: none on the question itself. The orientation negative was
  checked against known positives as recorded above.

## Authorization gate

No grant covers reading a billing, CRM, or revenue system, and no such system is even
reachable from this session. Reachability would not have been authorization in any case.
Per the gate, the already-authorized subset was done (local read-only orientation and a
search of the user's own connected Drive); the rest is reported as work that needs
authorization rather than attempted.

## Tests

| id | Hypothesis | Preregistered prediction | Method | Outcome | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | H1 | Re-cut on equal-length windows removes the majority of the gap | Re-aggregate transactions on aligned windows | NOT_TESTED | — |
| T2 | H2 | Billable units fall | Decompose spend into units × effective rate | NOT_TESTED | — |
| T3 | H3 | Effective rate falls | Same decomposition, rate factor | NOT_TESTED | — |
| T4 | H4 | The delta concentrates in few components | Rank component contributions to the delta | NOT_TESTED | — |
| T5 | H5 | An offsetting increase appears in the account family | Sum spend across the parent/entity hierarchy | NOT_TESTED | — |

## Amendments

- 2026-08-11: none. Ledger created at Plan time; execution blocked before first collection.

## Conclusion

- Answer: **cannot be determined — no data.** The question is well-formed and the plan is
  preregistered, but no source describing Northgate Clinic exists in this environment.
- Per-hypothesis summary:

  | id | claim | status | basis |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | H1 | data-artifact | UNRESOLVED | no test run — no source |
  | H2 | descriptive | UNRESOLVED | no test run — no source |
  | H3 | descriptive | UNRESOLVED | no test run — no source |
  | H4 | descriptive | UNRESOLVED | no test run — no source |
  | H5 | causal | UNRESOLVED | no test run — no source |
